_how_to_edit: Every CASA audit item must appear exactly once. status = verified | not_applicable | pending. verified needs evidence (test:<fn>, lint:<rule>, tool:<name>, file:<path>) or an attestation {by,date,artifact}. not_applicable needs reason + reopen_if regexes that fail the gate if matching code appears. pending needs a blocker and fails release builds (CASA_STRICT=1). After editing run: python3 scripts/casa_check.py render

requirements.title: Authentication is resistant to brute force attacks
requirements.notes: Google sign-in: credentials are entered at Google, the only sign-in Hadal offers by default. Email + password accounts are off unless PASSWORD_AUTH_ENABLED=true (the default and the production setting are off); while off, /api/auth/register, /api/auth/password-login and /api/auth/password don't exist and return 404 before any handler runs (test:password_accounts_are_off_unless_enabled). The controls below still apply, and are tested, if they are switched on. Email + password sign-in: /api/auth/register and /api/auth/password-login share the per-IP auth limit (default 10/min, burst 5) with the Google endpoints, and password-login is also limited per account (10 attempts, then 1 per 3 min, keyed by email whether or not it exists), so guessing one account from many IPs is slowed too. Both limiters fail closed. The push endpoint has no credentials to guess (it checks a Google signature) and sits behind the global per-IP limit; a forged key ID makes the backend refetch Google's keys at most once a minute, whether or not Google answers.

requirements.title: System generated initial passwords or activation codes are securely random and expire quickly
requirements.reason: The app issues no passwords or activation codes; sign-in is delegated to Google.

requirements.title: Passwords are stored in a form resistant to offline attacks
requirements.notes: Email + password accounts are off unless PASSWORD_AUTH_ENABLED=true (the default and the production setting are off); while off, /api/auth/register, /api/auth/password-login and /api/auth/password don't exist and return 404 before any handler runs (test:password_accounts_are_off_unless_enabled). The controls below still apply, and are tested, if they are switched on. Passwords are hashed with Argon2id (m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1, OWASP's minimum, pinned in auth/password.rs) with a 128-bit random salt per password, as a PHC string. The users table only accepts '$argon2id$' values. Hashing runs on a blocking thread. Policy: 12-128 characters, no composition rules (ASVS 2.1). Unknown emails still cost one verification, so timing doesn't reveal accounts. Caveat: in the production configuration (PASSWORD_AUTH_ENABLED=false) Hadal stores no passwords at all, since sign-in is Google-only; this item is verified for the opt-in password path, which must not be enabled in production without re-reviewing it. The Argon2id cost is OWASP's floor, not tuned to the production host. Not yet: breached-password check (ASVS 2.1.7).

requirements.title: Default credentials are not present on publicly exposed interfaces
requirements.notes: Migrations seed no accounts. .env.example ships an empty POSTGRES_PASSWORD, and docker-compose refuses to start until it is set. Postgres binds to 127.0.0.1 only.

requirements.title: Out of band verifier expires in a reasonable timeframe
requirements.reason: No SMS, email or other out-of-band verification codes are issued.

requirements.title: Out of band verifier is only used once
Out of band verifier is securely random
Out of band verifier is resistant to brute force attacks
Passwords, session tokens and API keys are not exposed in URL parameters
Users can log out; logout or expiry invalidates all stateful session tokens, including refresh tokens
requirements.notes: Sessions are server-side rows. POST /api/auth/logout deletes the row and clears the cookie. Idle (30 min) and absolute (12 h) expiry are checked against the database clock on every request. The only tokens the app issues are these session rows. Google refresh tokens are kept only for linked Gmail mailboxes, AES-256-GCM encrypted; they are delegated grants to Google, not app sessions, and are revoked at Google and deleted when the mailbox is unlinked. Sign-in never keeps Google tokens. An open live-update stream checks its session every 20 s without sliding the idle window, and ends on logout or expiry, so an open tab doesn't keep a session alive and a signed-out user stops getting events.

requirements.title: Other sessions can be terminated after a password change or reset
requirements.notes: Email + password accounts are off unless PASSWORD_AUTH_ENABLED=true (the default and the production setting are off); while off, /api/auth/register, /api/auth/password-login and /api/auth/password don't exist and return 404 before any handler runs (test:password_accounts_are_off_unless_enabled). The controls below still apply, and are tested, if they are switched on. POST /api/auth/password (signed in, current password required, throttled per IP and per account) updates the Argon2id hash and deletes every session of the user in one transaction, then issues a fresh session to this browser only. Google accounts have no password here; their credential changes happen at Google. A future password reset must do the same (CLAUDE.md).

requirements.title: Non-revocable stateless authentication tokens expire within 24 hours
requirements.notes: No stateless tokens are issued. Sessions are revocable anyway, and the config refuses an absolute lifetime above 24 h.

requirements.title: Cookie-based session tokens have the Secure attribute
requirements.notes: Cookies are built only in backend/src/auth/cookies.rs, always with Secure and the __Host- prefix.

requirements.title: Cookie-based session tokens have the HttpOnly attribute
requirements.notes: Cookies are built only in backend/src/auth/cookies.rs, always HttpOnly. The SPA never reads them.

requirements.title: Session tokens are used rather than static API secrets and keys
requirements.notes: Each sign-in gets its own random 256-bit session token (only its SHA-256 is stored). There are no static API keys for clients.

requirements.title: Stateless session tokens are protected against tampering, replay, null cipher and key substitution
requirements.reason: Sessions are opaque random tokens looked up server-side; no stateless (JWT/PASETO) session tokens exist. Google's ID token is consumed once at sign-in and never used as a session (see 3.2.1).

requirements.title: A full valid session or re-authentication is required before sensitive transactions or account changes
requirements.notes: Every state-changing endpoint sits behind require_session. The account changes Hadal offers are signed-in, JSON-only POSTs: renaming (POST /api/auth/profile, only first and last name) and, only if email + password accounts are switched on (off by default), changing the password (POST /api/auth/password, which also requires the current password and signs out other sessions). The Google account itself is managed at Google.

requirements.title: Least-privilege access control rules are enforced on a trusted service layer
requirements.notes: Deny by default: the /api/mail scope and /api/auth/gmail/connect are wrapped in require_session, and handlers take AuthUser, which refuses if the middleware didn't run. Only /api/health and the sign-in endpoints are public. Linking a mailbox never creates a sign-in account for it. Gmail push (optional, GMAIL_PUSH_*): POST /api/gmail/push is called by Google's Cloud Pub/Sub, not a browser, so it has no session. Instead every request must carry a token Google signed (RS256, verified against Google's published keys, fetched from a fixed URL) for our subscription's exact audience and service account, current and with a verified email; anything else is a 401 before the body is used. With push off the route is a 404. A genuine notification only names a Gmail address: it queues syncs of the watched mailbox rows with that address, each under the owner stored on its row, and the sync reads from Gmail with that row's own grant. The live-update stream GET /api/mail/events is inside the /api/mail session scope and carries only the owner's own mailbox IDs.

requirements.title: User and data attributes used by access controls cannot be manipulated by end users
requirements.notes: Every request body struct uses deny_unknown_fields, so server-controlled fields such as id, created_at and (later) owner_id cannot be mass-assigned. Registration rejects extra fields such as id, password_hash and google_sub; the profile update takes only first_name and last_name (not email or any flag). Query strings are typed the same way: the message list accepts only account (a UUID) and label (ALL, one of ten Gmail system labels, or a Label_<id> user label ID), and anything else is a 400.

requirements.title: Access controls fail securely, including when an exception occurs
Sensitive resources are protected against IDOR on create, read, update and delete
requirements.notes: Every mail_accounts and mail_messages query is scoped by owner_id from the session, never from the request (lint:notes-owner-scope covers both tables, and still flags the removed notes table if it comes back). mail_messages has a composite foreign key to (mailbox id, owner_id), so a message can't belong to someone else's mailbox. The message list's optional account filter is ANDed with owner_id, so another user's mailbox id matches nothing. Another user's mailbox, message or attachment returns the same 404 as a missing one; an attachment download is picked by its position in the owner's own encrypted record, never by a Gmail ID from the request. The Gmail link callback takes the user from the single-use pending row, not the request. Push sync: the one lookup not keyed by a session's user is by the Gmail address a Google-signed notification names (mail::watched_mailboxes). It returns (mailbox, owner) pairs from our rows; every query after it, and the sync itself, is scoped by that stored owner_id. Live events go only to the owner's own streams.

requirements.title: Strong anti-CSRF protects authenticated functionality; anti-automation or anti-CSRF protects unauthenticated functionality
requirements.notes: Session cookie is SameSite=Strict. State-changing endpoints (including logout) accept only application/json, which a cross-site form cannot send without a CORS preflight, and no CORS is granted. Sign-in CSRF is blocked by the state check (3.2.2).

requirements.title: Directory browsing is disabled
Only secure OAuth 2.0 flows (Authorization Code, with PKCE) are used; implicit and password grants are not
requirements.notes: Authorization Code + PKCE (S256) with a nonce, for both sign-in and Gmail linking (one registered redirect URI; the pending row says which flow it is). The ID token comes straight from Google's token endpoint over verified TLS, so per OIDC Core §3.1.3.7 the TLS check stands in for the signature; iss, aud, exp, iat, nonce and email_verified are all checked. Sign-in discards Google's access and refresh tokens. Linking keeps only the refresh token, encrypted (see 6.7.1), and is refused unless the gmail.readonly scope was actually granted. Sign-in never requests Gmail scopes.

requirements.title: redirect_uri and state are validated during OAuth authorization
requirements.notes: redirect_uri is fixed in config, validated at startup (https, exact path, no query) and never read from the request. state is random, stored server-side under a __Host- login cookie, compared in constant time and single-use (replay test). The RFC 9207 iss parameter is checked when present.

requirements.title: Application administrative interfaces use multi-factor authentication
requirements.reason: The application exposes no administrative interface.

requirements.title: TLS is enforced for all connections (TLS 1.2+, secure cipher suites)
requirements.notes: nginx terminates TLS 1.2/1.3 only with forward-secret AEAD suites (Mozilla intermediate), no session tickets. Port 80 only answers 301 to https://hadalspace.com (the fixed canonical host, never the request's Host) for Hadal's own names, plus the ACME challenge; unknown host names get no response on 80 and 421 on 443. The TLS settings are set once for every server, so a client that sends no SNI gets the same hardened handshake (check-tls.sh checks the no-SNI case too). HSTS (2 years in the image; 5 minutes in local compose so localhost isn't pinned) is sent exactly once on every response, including the proxied API. scripts/check-tls.sh checks all of this against the running stack in CI (refuses TLS 1.0/1.1 and non-FS/CBC suites), and ZAP scans over HTTPS. The OAuth redirect URI must be https except on localhost. Production (docker-compose.prod.yml) serves hadalspace.com with a Let's Encrypt certificate renewed by certbot; port 80 serves only the ACME challenge and the redirect. Before the assessment, run check-tls.sh against hadalspace.com and attach an SSL Labs report.

requirements.title: Connections to and from the server use trusted TLS certificates
requirements.notes: Backend to Postgres: TLS with sslmode=verify-full against a private CA (certificate and host name 'db' checked); the backend refuses to start with a non-local DATABASE_URL that isn't verify-full. Postgres requires TLS 1.2+ for every network connection (pg_hba hostssl only, hostnossl rejected); check-tls.sh confirms every live connection is TLS and a plaintext one is refused. Backend to Google: rustls, Mozilla roots, https only. nginx to backend is plain HTTP inside the private compose network, which never leaves the host. For a managed database use its CA as sslrootcert.

requirements.title: No weak cryptography affecting confidential data
requirements.notes: Refresh tokens and imported mail (summary, body, attachment names/types/sizes, and the user's Gmail label names) are encrypted with AES-256-GCM (ring) under DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY, with a random 96-bit nonce from the OS CSPRNG per value. Attachment files are not stored: they are fetched from Gmail when downloaded.

requirements.title: Cryptographic modules fail securely; no padding oracles
requirements.notes: TLS is the only encryption, and nginx allows only AEAD suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) on TLS 1.2 plus TLS 1.3, so there are no CBC suites to build a padding oracle on; check-tls.sh confirms CBC and non-forward-secret suites are refused. At rest, the app encrypts Google refresh tokens and imported mail with AES-256-GCM from ring (backend/src/crypto.rs): authenticated encryption with no CBC and no padding, so there is no padding oracle. A wrong key, wrong associated data (another row), tampering or truncation is an error, and no partial plaintext is returned. Otherwise the app hashes (SHA-256 for tokens, Argon2id for passwords), and Argon2 verification fails closed (a malformed hash is a mismatch). rustls (backend to Google and Postgres) has no CBC suites.

requirements.title: Protect against HTTP parameter pollution
requirements.notes: JSON bodies: serde rejects a repeated key with 400 (duplicate_json_keys_are_rejected). Query strings are parsed only through typed web::Query<T> (lint:raw-query-string forbids reading query_string() by hand), so a repeated parameter fails deserialization and the QueryConfig handler answers 400 "invalid query string" instead of letting the first or last value win (duplicate_query_params_are_rejected, on /api/mail/messages).

requirements.title: URL redirects and forwards are limited to allowlisted URLs
requirements.notes: Every redirect has a fixed target. Backend: only through auth::redirect(), to Google's authorization endpoint (an AuthorizeUrl only GoogleClient can build) or constant same-origin paths; nothing comes from the request. nginx: both HTTP->HTTPS redirects (port 80, and plain HTTP sent to the TLS port via error_page 497) go to CANONICAL_HOST (hadalspace.com in production), never the request's Host header. Requests for any other host name hit default servers that close the connection (port 80, 444) or answer 421 Misdirected Request (port 443, with the same hardened TLS settings, so clients that send no SNI still work), whether the foreign name came in the SNI or only in the Host header. So the edge can't be used as an open redirect or serve the app under someone else's name. check-tls.sh checks this on the running stack in CI: no redirect to a foreign Host on port 80, 421 for a foreign SNI, and no app response for a foreign Host with the right SNI.

requirements.title: No eval() or other dynamic code execution
Protect against template injection
requirements.reason: No server-side templating. The UI is compiled SolidJS JSX, which escapes text by default.

requirements.title: Prevent server-side request forgery
requirements.notes: All outbound HTTP is in backend/src/auth/google.rs, to Google's constant endpoints: token (code exchange and refresh), revoke, and the Gmail API under https://gmail.googleapis.com/gmail/v1/users/me/ (message list, messages, and message attachments). No host or URL comes from user input; Gmail message IDs from Google are checked to be plain alphanumeric, and attachment IDs plain base64url, before they go into a path segment; the only labels ever sent as a list filter are our fixed system-label constants or user label IDs Gmail itself returned from users.labels.list, re-checked against a strict pattern before use. User label names and colours from Gmail are cleaned and validated before they are stored. Responses are size-capped (attachments at Gmail's 25 MB limit). Redirects and proxies are disabled on the client; lint:outbound-http rejects HTTP clients anywhere else. Gmail push adds users.watch, users.stop, users.history.list and users.getProfile under the same fixed Gmail API base, and Google's signing keys from the fixed https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs. History IDs are digits only and page tokens re-checked before they go into a query string; the watched topic is fixed configuration, checked at start-up. Nothing in a push notification is used to build a request.

requirements.title: Protect against XPath or XML injection
requirements.reason: No XML is parsed or produced.

requirements.title: Context-aware output escaping protects against reflected, stored and DOM XSS
requirements.notes: API: JSON only, nosniff, CSP default-src 'none', set by the backend alone (nginx adds no headers to proxied /api/ responses). UI: Solid escapes interpolations, raw HTML sinks are banned, strict CSP from nginx. Imported mail is never rendered as HTML: HTML-only bodies are reduced to plain text on the server, and the UI shows bodies as text in a <pre>. Attachments are only ever downloads: always application/octet-stream with Content-Disposition: attachment (whatever type the email claims), under the API's nosniff and CSP, so a file from an email can't run as a page on our origin. File names are cleaned at import and encoded in the header so they can't inject parameters.

requirements.title: Protect against database injection
requirements.notes: All SQL is static text with sqlx bind parameters.

requirements.title: Protect against OS command injection
Protect against local and remote file inclusion
Uploads are limited to expected types and never executed
Only components without known exploitable vulnerabilities are used
Debug modes are disabled in production
The Origin header is not used for authentication or access control decisions
The application is not susceptible to subdomain takeover
requirements.blocker: Production is hadalspace.com and www.hadalspace.com (docker-compose.prod.yml). Before assessment, audit the hadalspace.com DNS zone for dangling CNAMEs or records pointing at hosts you no longer control, and record it as an attestation.

requirements.title: Credentials and payment details are not logged; session tokens appear in logs only hashed
requirements.notes: Session tokens are never logged; only their SHA-256 is stored. Sign-in failures log a reason code, not the code, state or tokens. Secret config values use a redacting Secret type. Passwords are never logged or returned: the request structs don't derive Debug, and failed sign-ins log only that they failed.

requirements.title: Browser storage is securely cleared during logout
requirements.notes: The SPA keeps nothing in browser storage; the session lives only in an HttpOnly cookie, which logout clears (Max-Age=0) and deletes server-side.

requirements.title: Access tokens, API keys and other server-side secrets are stored securely
requirements.blocker: In code, secrets come only from the environment, .env is git-ignored, and gitleaks runs on every commit. Google refresh tokens and imported mail are stored AES-256-GCM encrypted, bound to their row; access tokens are only held in memory. Production still needs a secrets manager (encrypted, access-controlled, audited) holding DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEY and the OAuth client secret; record it as an attestation.

requirements.title: Webhook communications use HTTPS with TLS 1.2+ only
requirements.notes: Inbound: Pub/Sub delivers Gmail push to our HTTPS endpoint only. The configured audience must be an https URL (checked at start-up), and nginx serves it with TLS 1.2/1.3 and the same cipher policy as the rest of the site (4.1.1). Hadal sends no webhooks.

requirements.title: Webhook providers verify endpoint ownership before delivering events
requirements.reason: Hadal sends no webhooks, so it is never a webhook provider. The one it receives, Gmail push through Google's Cloud Pub/Sub, has a fixed endpoint we configure in Google Cloud ourselves (no user-supplied callback URLs); see 7.1.1 and 7.2.x.

requirements.title: Webhook payloads are authenticated with HMAC-SHA256 or stronger
requirements.notes: The one webhook Hadal receives, Gmail push via Cloud Pub/Sub (POST /api/gmail/push, off unless GMAIL_PUSH_* is set), is authenticated with an RS256 signature (RSA, keys of 2048 bits or more, SHA-256) by Google over an OIDC token bound to our push URL (aud) and our subscription's service account (email). That is an asymmetric signature at least as strong as HMAC-SHA256, and it needs no shared secret. Only RS256 is accepted. The token, not the payload, is signed; the payload is used only to name a mailbox, and the sync it starts reads everything from Gmail with Hadal's own grant.

requirements.title: Webhook signature verification uses timing-safe comparison
requirements.notes: Gmail push (POST /api/gmail/push, off unless GMAIL_PUSH_* is set) is the one webhook Hadal receives: Google's Cloud Pub/Sub delivers Gmail's change notifications. It is not signed with a shared secret: each request carries an OIDC token Google signs with its own RSA key (RS256), verified with ring against Google's published keys from the fixed https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs. Verification is an asymmetric signature check (ring's RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 SHA-256 verify, keys of 2048 bits or more), not a comparison of a secret MAC, so there is no MAC to compare; only RS256 is accepted, so `none` and HMAC algorithms (alg confusion) are refused. The audience claim is compared with a constant-time comparison (token::ct_eq). A failed check is a 401 before the body is read. Hadal sends no webhooks.

requirements.title: Webhook payloads include replay protection via signed timestamps
requirements.notes: Gmail push (POST /api/gmail/push, off unless GMAIL_PUSH_* is set) is the one webhook Hadal receives: Google's Cloud Pub/Sub delivers Gmail's change notifications. It is not signed with a shared secret: each request carries an OIDC token Google signs with its own RSA key (RS256), verified with ring against Google's published keys from the fixed https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs. Replay protection: the token's exp and iat are inside the signed payload and checked (60 s clock skew); Google issues each token for at most an hour. Within that hour a replayed notification can do nothing new: it only names a mailbox, its historyId is ignored, and the sync it queues reads changes from Gmail starting at the point Hadal stored, so a repeat finds nothing to change (the test syncs twice and the second finds no changes).

requirements.title: Webhook providers mitigate SSRF for user-supplied callback URLs
requirements.reason: Hadal sends no webhooks, so it is never a webhook provider. The one it receives, Gmail push through Google's Cloud Pub/Sub, has a fixed endpoint we configure in Google Cloud ourselves (no user-supplied callback URLs); see 7.1.1 and 7.2.x.

requirements.title: Webhook signing secrets are not hardcoded or stored in version control
requirements.notes: Gmail push (POST /api/gmail/push, off unless GMAIL_PUSH_* is set) is the one webhook Hadal receives: Google's Cloud Pub/Sub delivers Gmail's change notifications. It is not signed with a shared secret: each request carries an OIDC token Google signs with its own RSA key (RS256), verified with ring against Google's published keys from the fixed https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs. There is no webhook signing secret to store: Google holds the private key, and Hadal only fetches Google's public keys at run time. The push settings (topic, audience URL, service account email, all non-secret) come from the environment and are validated at start-up. The test-only RSA key in backend/src/auth/testdata is used by tests alone and never trusted by the app (docs/casa/exceptions.md).
